missing_spec_content.spec_text: investigate the effectiveness of different materials as thermal insulators and the factors that may affect the thermal insulation properties of a material.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson covers only the first half of the practical: comparing materials (keyPoints[3].content, 'The independent variable is the material'). It treats thickness only as a control variable. It never shows how to investigate a factor such as thickness or number of layers as the independent variable.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Investigate thermal conductivity using rods of different materials.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not mention comparing thermal conductivity using rods of different materials.

above_gcse.text: How well a material conducts energy; the higher it is, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction
above_gcse.why: The spec says 'Students do not need to know the definition of thermal conductivity.' The lesson presents a definition as a key term to learn. Only the relationship to the rate of energy transfer is required.

above_gcse.text: Thermal conductivity: this tells you how well a material conducts energy.
above_gcse.why: This is the same issue. The spec explicitly says the definition is not required, yet the lesson presents one.

above_gcse.text: Sankey diagrams are drawn to scale. The width of each arrow shows the amount of energy. All the arrows must add up to the input.
above_gcse.why: Sankey diagrams are not part of the supplied specification section 4.1.2.1. They are presented as exam content without support from these sections.

factual_errors.correction: 'Electrical' is not an energy store in the GCSE stores-and-pathways model. Energy is transferred electrically, which is a pathway. For the bulb, kettle and motor, the input is energy transferred electrically from a store such as a chemical store in a power station or battery.

factual_errors.text: A light bulb transfers electrical energy into two outputs. These are useful light energy and wasted thermal energy.
factual_errors.correction: Light and electrical energy are not stores. Energy is transferred electrically to the bulb. It is transferred usefully by light (radiation) and dissipated by heating to the thermal store of the surroundings.

factual_errors.text: electrical resistance in wires: electrical energy → thermal energy. This is how a kettle heats water.
factual_errors.correction: Heating the water is the useful transfer in a kettle, not dissipation. The lesson itself says this in tables[0] and checkpoints[1]. Using it as an example of dissipation, i.e. energy 'stored in less useful ways', is wrong.

factual_errors.text: The words 'lost' and 'used up' are banned in physics.
factual_errors.correction: 'Energy loss' and 'heat loss' are widely used in physics to mean energy transferred out of a system. The lesson uses them itself: keyPoints[1].keyTerms[2].def 'heat loss', keyPoints[3].writeBullets[2] 'heat loss through the roof', tables[0] 'Thermal lost to surroundings'. The real point is that energy is not destroyed.
